a x^{2} + b x + c = a(x + b/(2a))^{2} +.title: Completing the square
a x^{2} + b x + c = a(x + b/(2a))^{2} +.about: Since (x + p)^{2} = x^{2} + 2px + p^{2}, the x coefficient fixes p as half of it, and you subtract p^{2} to keep the value. This shows the vertex at once, gives the quadratic formula, and is how integrals like ∫ dx/(x^{2} + 6x + 13) are done.

example.problem: Write x^{2} + 6x + 5 in vertex form.

assumptions: Common slip: factor a out of the x^{2} and x terms first when a ≠ 1

r_{1} + r_{2} = −b/a, r_{1} r_{2} = c/a.title: Vieta's formulas: sum and product of the roots
r_{1} + r_{2} = −b/a, r_{1} r_{2} = c/a.about: Multiply out a(x − r_{1})(x − r_{2}) = ax^{2} − a(r_{1} + r_{2})x + a r_{1} r_{2} and match coefficients with ax^{2} + bx + c. The roots add to −b/a and multiply to c/a, real or complex. Handy for checking roots and for building a quadratic from its roots.
related: the monic quadratic with those roots

example.problem: Without solving, find the sum and product of the roots of 2x^{2} − 7x + 3 = 0.

assumptions: Common slip: the sum is −b/a, with a minus
In a characteristic equation r^{2} + 2ζω_{n} r + ω_{n}^{2}, the roots multiply to ω_{n}^{2}

p(x) = (x − r) q(x) + p(r).title: Remainder and factor theorems
p(x) = (x − r) q(x) + p(r).about: Dividing p by x − r leaves a quotient q and a constant remainder R (lower degree than x − r). Put x = r: the first term vanishes, so R = p(r). Hence x − r is a factor exactly when p(r) = 0, which is how roots are tested and polynomials factored.

example.problem: Is x − 2 a factor of p(x) = x^{3} − 3x^{2} + 4?
steps: The remainder is 0, so x − 2 is a factor: p(x) = (x − 2)(x^{2} − x − 2)

assumptions: Common slip: for the factor x + 2, test r = −2, not 2
Rational roots must be ± (factor of the constant)/(factor of the leading coefficient); try those first

log_{b}(x) = y ⇔ b^{y} = x.title: What a logarithm is
log_{b}(x) = y ⇔ b^{y} = x.about: log_b(x) is the exponent you raise b to in order to get x. Turning a log equation into exponent form (or back) is the first step in solving most of them.
assumptions: b > 0 and b ≠ 1; x > 0
Common slip: log of a negative number or 0 has no real value; check answers against x > 0

example.problem: Solve log_{2}(x) = 5.

log_{b}(x/y) = log_{b}(x) − log_{b}(y).title: Quotient rule for logarithms
log_{b}(x/y) = log_{b}(x) − log_{b}(y).about: The log of a quotient is the difference of the logs, because dividing powers of b subtracts their exponents.
assumptions: x > 0 and y > 0

y = a f(b(x − h)) + k.title: Transformations of a graph
y = a f(b(x − h)) + k.about: Starting from y = f(x): h shifts the graph right, k shifts it up, a stretches it vertically (and flips it if negative), and b squeezes it horizontally by 1/b (flipping it if negative).
vars: vertical stretch; a < 0 reflects in the x-axis
horizontal squeeze by 1/b; b < 0 reflects in the y-axis

example.problem: Describe y = −2(x − 3)^{2} + 1 starting from y = x^{2}.
example.answer: a downward parabola, vertex (3, 1), twice as steep

assumptions: Common slip: x − h shifts right, opposite to the sign you see; y = f(x + 2) moves left 2
Factor b out first: f(2x − 6) = f(2(x − 3)) shifts right 3, not 6
Changes inside the brackets act on x (horizontal, inverted); outside act on y (vertical, as written)
related: vertex form, the case f = x^{2}

f(−x) = f(x).title: Even function
f(−x) = f(x).about: A function is even when replacing x by −x leaves it unchanged; its graph is mirrored across the y-axis. The name comes from powers: x^{2}, x^{4} are even, and so is cos x, whose series has only even powers. Payoff: ∫_{−a}^{a} f dx = 2∫_{0}^{a} f dx, and an even signal's Fourier series has only cosines.

example.problem: Is f(x) = x^{4} − 3x^{2} even?

assumptions: Most functions are neither: e^{x} is neither, but any f splits into an even part (f(x) + f(−x))/2 and an odd part (f(x) − f(−x))/2
Common slip: testing only one value of x; the equation must hold for every x

f(−x) = −f(x).title: Odd function
f(−x) = −f(x).about: A function is odd when replacing x by −x flips its sign; its graph is unchanged by a half turn about the origin, so it passes through (0, 0) if defined there. Examples: x^{3}, sin x, tan x. Payoff: ∫_{−a}^{a} f dx = 0, and an odd signal's Fourier series has only sines.

example.problem: Evaluate ∫ (x^{3} + x) dx from −2 to 2.
steps: The areas left and right of 0 cancel

assumptions: Odd × odd is even, odd × even is odd (like multiplying signs)
Common slip: adding a constant breaks oddness: x^{3} + 1 is neither

(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).title: Composition of functions
(f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).about: Apply g first, then f to its result: read right to left. Order matters, since f(g(x)) is usually not g(f(x)). Spotting the inner and outer function is the first step of the chain rule.

example.problem: With f(x) = x^{2} and g(x) = x + 1, find (f ∘ g)(3) and (g ∘ f)(3).

assumptions: Domain: x must be in g's domain and g(x) in f's (√(x − 1) ∘ ... needs g(x) ≥ 1)
Common slip: (f ∘ g)(x) is not f(x) · g(x)
related: composing with an inverse gives back x

f(f^{−1}(x)) = x.title: Inverse function
f(f^{−1}(x)) = x.about: The inverse undoes f: put f^{−1}'s output into f and you get back where you started. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, and solve for y. Its graph is f's mirrored across y = x.

example.problem: F = 1.8C + 32 turns Celsius into Fahrenheit. Find the inverse and convert 98.6 °F.

assumptions: f must be one-to-one; otherwise restrict its domain first (x^{2} with x ≥ 0 has inverse √x)
Common slip: f^{−1}(x) is not 1/f(x)

(f(x + h) − f(x))/h.title: Difference quotient: average rate of change
(f(x + h) − f(x))/h.about: The slope of the secant line from x to x + h: how fast f changes on average over a step h. As h shrinks to 0 it becomes the derivative f′(x).
assumptions: f defined at x and x + h
Common slip: expanding f(x + h) as f(x) + h; substitute x + h for every x
Cancel h algebraically before letting h → 0
related: the same slope between two points

example.problem: Simplify the difference quotient of f(x) = x^{2}.
example.answer: 2x + h, which tends to 2x as h → 0

r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}.title: Polar radius from rectangular coordinates
r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}.about: A point (x, y) lies at distance r = √(x² + y²) from the origin, by Pythagoras. Pair it with θ = atan2(y, x) for the angle.

example.problem: Convert (−3, 4) to polar.

assumptions: Common slip: θ = tan^{−1}(y/x) misses the quadrant; use atan2(y, x)

c^{2} = a^{2} − b^{2}.title: Foci of an ellipse
c^{2} = a^{2} − b^{2}.about: For x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with a > b, the foci sit on the long axis at (±c, 0). Every point on the ellipse has distances to the two foci that add to 2a.

example.problem: Find the foci of x^{2}/25 + y^{2}/9 = 1.

assumptions: a > b > 0; if b > a the foci are on the y-axis at (0, ±c) with c^{2} = b^{2} − a^{2}
Common slip: the hyperbola uses c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}; the ellipse subtracts, so c < a

c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}.title: Foci of a hyperbola
c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}.about: For x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 the foci are at (±c, 0) with c² = a² + b². Every point on the hyperbola has distances to the foci that differ by 2a.

example.problem: Find the foci of x^{2}/9 − y^{2}/16 = 1.

assumptions: Common slip: the ellipse uses c^{2} = a^{2} − b^{2}; the hyperbola adds
a goes with the positive term: for y^{2}/a^{2} − x^{2}/b^{2} = 1 the foci are at (0, ±c)

y = ±(b/a) x.title: Asymptotes of a hyperbola
y = ±(b/a) x.about: Far from the centre the 1 in x^{2}/a^{2} − y^{2}/b^{2} = 1 is negligible, so y^{2} ≈ b^{2}x^{2}/a^{2}: the hyperbola hugs the lines y = ±(b/a)x. Sketch the box of half-width a and half-height b; its diagonals are the asymptotes.

example.problem: Give the asymptotes of x^{2}/4 − y^{2}/9 = 1.

assumptions: Common slip: for y^{2}/a^{2} − x^{2}/b^{2} = 1 (opening up and down) the slopes are ±a/b

x^{2} = 4 p y.title: Parabola opening up (focus and directrix)
x^{2} = 4 p y.about: Every point is equally far from the focus (0, p) and the directrix y = −p. Negative p opens down. Light from the focus reflects parallel to the axis, which is why dishes are parabolic.

example.problem: A dish follows x^{2} = 8y. Where is its focus?

e = c/a.title: Eccentricity of a conic
e = c/a.about: How stretched a conic is: 0 for a circle, between 0 and 1 for an ellipse, 1 for a parabola, more than 1 for a hyperbola. For an orbit it sets the shape of the ellipse.

example.problem: An ellipse has a = 5 and b = 3. Find e.

assumptions: c and a from the same conic: c^{2} = a^{2} − b^{2} for an ellipse, a^{2} + b^{2} for a hyperbola

dT/dt = −k (T − T_{a}).title: Newton's law of cooling as an ODE
dT/dt = −k (T − T_{a}).about: A body's temperature changes at a rate proportional to its difference from the surroundings. The solution is T = T_{a} + (T_{0} − T_{a}) e^{−kt}.
assumptions: Ambient temperature constant; the body has one uniform temperature (lumped)
Common slip: decaying T to 0 instead of to T_{a}

example.problem: Coffee at 90 °C sits in a 20 °C room with k = 0.05 /min. What is it after 10 min?

dy/dt + p y = q y^{n}.title: Bernoulli differential equation
dy/dt + p y = q y^{n}.about: A nonlinear first-order equation that the substitution v = y^{1−n} turns into a linear one: dv/dt + (1 − n) p v = (1 − n) q. Solve that with an integrating factor.
assumptions: n ≠ 0, 1 (for those it is already linear)
Why it works: dividing by y^{n} gives y^{−n} y′ + p y^{1−n} = q, and y^{−n}y′ is v′/(1 − n)
Common slip: forgetting the factor (1 − n) on both p and q
related: integrating factor for the linear v equation

example.problem: Solve dy/dt − y = −y^{2}.
steps: dv/dt + (1 − n)p v = (1 − n)q gives dv/dt + v = 1
example.answer: y = 1/(1 + C e^{−t}), the logistic curve

M dx + N dy = 0.title: Exact equation
M dx + N dy = 0.about: If ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x, the left side is the total differential of some F(x, y). Find F from F_x = M and F_y = N; the solution is F(x, y) = C.

example.problem: Solve (2xy) dx + (x^{2} + 1) dy = 0.

assumptions: M, N and their first partials continuous on a simply connected region
Common slip: skipping the exactness test, or dropping h(y) when integrating M
Not exact? An integrating factor that depends on x alone exists if (M_y − N_x)/N depends only on x
related: the same test for a conservative field
separable equations are a special case

y′′ + 2ζω_{n} y′ + ω_{n}^{2} y = 0.title: Damped oscillator in standard form
y′′ + 2ζω_{n} y′ + ω_{n}^{2} y = 0.about: Dividing m y′′ + c y′ + k y = 0 by m. ζ < 1 oscillates (underdamped), ζ = 1 is critically damped, ζ > 1 creeps back (overdamped). The roots are r = −ζω_{n} ± ω_{n}√(ζ² − 1).

example.problem: y′′ + 4y′ + 16y = 0. Find ω_n and ζ.

assumptions: Linear, constant coefficients, no forcing
ω_{d} = ω_{n}√(1 − ζ^{2}) is the ringing frequency when ζ < 1
Common slip: ω_{n} is not the frequency you see oscillating; that is ω_{d} = ω_{n}√(1 − ζ^{2})
related: a y′′ + b y′ + c y = 0
the general form: 2ζω_{n} = b/a, ω_{n}^{2} = c/a
Complex, α ± jβ ‖ y = e^{αt} (c_{1} cos(βt) + c_{2} sin(βt))

a t^{2} y′′ + b t y′ + c y = 0.title: Euler-Cauchy equation
a t^{2} y′′ + b t y′ + c y = 0.about: Each derivative is multiplied by the matching power of t, so y = t^{r} works. Distinct real r give t^{r₁} and t^{r₂}; a repeated r gives t^{r} and t^{r} ln t; complex α ± jβ give t^{α} cos(β ln t) and t^{α} sin(β ln t).
assumptions: Why t^{r}: each derivative lowers the power by one and each t raises it back, so the powers match; substitute t = e^{s} to turn it into a constant-coefficient equation
vars: power in the trial y = t^{r}

example.problem: Solve t^{2} y″ − 2y = 0.

a r(r − 1) + b r + c = 0.title: Indicial equation of an Euler-Cauchy equation
a r(r − 1) + b r + c = 0.about: With y = t^{r}, t y′ = r t^{r} and t^{2} y″ = r(r − 1) t^{r}: every term is a multiple of t^{r} (the equation is equidimensional), and dividing it out leaves this quadratic in r.
vars: coefficients of a t^{2} y′′ + b t y′ + c y = 0

example.problem: Find r for t^{2} y″ + 3t y′ + y = 0.
example.answer: r = −1 (repeated), so y = (c_{1} + c_{2} ln t)/t

assumptions: t > 0 (use |t| for t < 0)
Common slip: writing a r^{2} instead of a r(r − 1)
Distinct real r: t^{r_{1}}, t^{r_{2}}; repeated r: t^{r} and t^{r} ln t; complex α ± jβ: t^{α}cos(β ln t), t^{α}sin(β ln t)
related: a t^{2} y′′ + b t y′ + c y = 0

y = y_{h} + y_{p}.title: General solution of a linear nonhomogeneous ODE
y = y_{h} + y_{p}.about: The equation is linear, so the difference of any two solutions solves the unforced equation. Every solution is therefore one particular solution plus the homogeneous solution with its free constants.
vars: solves the equation with zero forcing
any one solution with the forcing

example.problem: Solve y″ + y = 2 with y(0) = 0, y′(0) = 0.
steps: y_{h} = c_{1} cos t + c_{2} sin t, y_{p} = 2

assumptions: The ODE is linear
Common slip: fitting the initial conditions to y_h before adding y_p; apply them to the whole y
related: a y′′ + b y′ + c y = 0

y_{p} = −y_{1} ∫ y_{2} g/W dt + y_{2} ∫.title: Variation of parameters
y_{p} = −y_{1} ∫ y_{2} g/W dt + y_{2} ∫.about: A particular solution for any forcing g, built from two homogeneous solutions y₁, y₂ and their Wronskian. Use it when undetermined coefficients has no guess (tan t, 1/t, …).
assumptions: The equation is written with y″ having coefficient 1
Why: let the constants in y_h vary, c_{1}(t)y_{1} + c_{2}(t)y_{2}, and require c_{1}′y_{1} + c_{2}′y_{2} = 0; solving for c′ gives these integrals
Common slip: using g before dividing by the y″ coefficient
vars: coefficients in y′′ + p y′ + q y = g

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ + y = sec t.
steps: y_{1} = cos t, y_{2} = sin t, W = cos^{2} t + sin^{2} t = 1
y_{p} = −cos t ∫ sin t sec t dt + sin t ∫ cos t sec t dt
∫ tan t dt = −ln|cos t| and ∫ 1 dt = t
example.answer: y_p = cos t ln|cos t| + t sin t

t^{n} ‖ A_{n} t^{n} + … + A_{1} t + A_{0.title: Undetermined coefficients: polynomial forcing
t^{n} ‖ A_{n} t^{n} + … + A_{1} t + A_{0.about: Derivatives of a polynomial are lower-degree polynomials, so a full polynomial of the same degree as the forcing closes up. Match coefficients from the top power down.

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ + y = t^{2}.
steps: Guess A t^{2} + B t + C: 2A + A t^{2} + B t + C = t^{2}

assumptions: Common slip: guessing just A t^{2} for a t^{2} forcing; include every lower power
If c = 0 (no y term) multiply by t; if b = c = 0 too, by t^{2}

e^{at} ‖ A e^{at}.title: Undetermined coefficients: exponential forcing
e^{at} ‖ A e^{at}.about: Every derivative of e^{at} is a multiple of e^{at}, so the guess survives the left side unchanged in shape and you match one coefficient: A = 1/P(a), where P is the characteristic polynomial. When a is itself a characteristic root, P(a) = 0 and that fails: multiply the guess by t (by t^{2} for a double root).

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ − y = e^{2t}.
steps: Characteristic roots ±1, so 2 is not a root
Guess A e^{2t}: (4A − A) e^{2t} = e^{2t}

assumptions: Linear, constant coefficients
Common slip: forgetting to compare a with the characteristic roots before guessing
related: the characteristic roots to compare with

cos(ωt), sin(ωt) ‖ A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt).title: Undetermined coefficients: sinusoidal forcing
cos(ωt), sin(ωt) ‖ A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt).about: Even if only a cosine drives the system, guess both cosine and sine, since damping shifts the phase. At resonance (jω a root) multiply by t.

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ + y′ = cos t, and its amplitude.
steps: (−A + B) cos t + (−B − A) sin t = cos t

assumptions: Linear, constant coefficients
Common slip: guessing only A cos(ωt); with any damping the response needs both
If jω is a root (undamped resonance), multiply by t
related: cos(ω_{0}t), sin(ω_{0}t) ‖ t (A cos(ω_{0}t) + B sin(ω_{0}t))
a cos(θ) + b sin(θ) = R cos(θ − φ)
to read amplitude and phase from A and B

e^{at} cos(ωt) ‖ e^{at} (A cos(ωt) + B s.title: Undetermined coefficients: decaying or growing sinusoid
e^{at} cos(ωt) ‖ e^{at} (A cos(ωt) + B s.about: Derivatives of e^{at} cos ωt only ever produce e^{at} cos ωt and e^{at} sin ωt, so a guess with both closes up under differentiation. Neater: drive with the complex e^{(a + jω)t}, solve as an exponential, and take the real part.

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ = e^{t} cos t.
steps: y″ of e^{t}(A cos t + B sin t) is e^{t}(2B cos t − 2A sin t)

assumptions: Linear, constant coefficients
Multiply by t if a ± jω is a characteristic root
Common slip: leaving out the sine term
related: cos(ωt), sin(ωt) ‖ A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt)
Complex, α ± jβ ‖ y = e^{αt} (c_{1} cos(βt) + c_{2} sin(βt))
the homogeneous solution to compare with

cos(ω_{0}t), sin(ω_{0}t) ‖ t (A cos(ω_{0.title: Undetermined coefficients: resonance, times t
cos(ω_{0}t), sin(ω_{0}t) ‖ t (A cos(ω_{0.about: When the forcing is at the natural frequency, A cos(ω_{0}t) + B sin(ω_{0}t) already solves the homogeneous equation and can't be a particular solution. Multiply the guess by t; undamped, the response then grows linearly without bound.
assumptions: ±jω_{0} are roots of the characteristic equation (undamped, y″ + ω_{0}^{2} y = g)
If they are double roots, multiply by t^{2}
related: cos(ωt), sin(ωt) ‖ A cos(ωt) + B sin(ωt)

example.problem: Find y_p for y″ + y = cos t.
steps: cos t solves y″ + y = 0, so guess t (A cos t + B sin t)
y_p″ + y_p = 2B cos t − 2A sin t = cos t

x = c_{1} v_{1} e^{λ_{1}t} + c_{2} v_{2}.title: General solution of x′ = A x (distinct eigenvalues)
x = c_{1} v_{1} e^{λ_{1}t} + c_{2} v_{2}.about: Each eigenvalue and eigenvector give a solution that moves along that eigenvector; the general solution adds them. Negative real parts mean the motion decays to rest.

steps: λ = 2 with v = (1, 0); λ = −1 with v = (0, 1)

assumptions: A has two distinct eigenvalues (so two independent eigenvectors)
Complex eigenvalues give oscillating solutions; take real and imaginary parts

u = X(x) T(t).title: Separation of variables
u = X(x) T(t).about: Guess a product of one-variable functions. A PDE such as the heat equation then splits into two ODEs linked by a separation constant, and the boundary conditions pick the allowed modes, which add up as a Fourier series.

example.problem: Separate u_t = α u_{xx} with u = 0 at x = 0 and x = L.
steps: X T′ = α X″ T, so T′/(αT) = X″/X = −λ
example.answer: u = Σ b_{n} sin(nπx/L) e^{−α(nπ/L)^{2} t}

assumptions: Linear, homogeneous PDE and boundary conditions
Why a constant: one side depends only on x and the other only on t, so both equal the same constant

u = f(x − ct) + g(x + ct).title: d'Alembert's solution of the wave equation
u = f(x − ct) + g(x + ct).about: Any solution of the 1D wave equation is a shape moving right plus a shape moving left, both at speed c. Why: in ξ = x − ct, η = x + ct the equation becomes ∂^{2}u/∂ξ∂η = 0, whose solution is any function of ξ plus any function of η. With u(x, 0) = φ and zero initial velocity, f = g = φ/2.
assumptions: Infinite string, no damping (ends reflect the waves)

example.problem: A long rope at rest has a small bump at x = 0. Waves travel at c = 300 m/s. Where is the bump after 2 ms?
steps: u = (φ(x − ct) + φ(x + ct))/2: two half-height bumps
example.answer: two half-height bumps at x = ±0.6 m

related: separation of variables, for finite strings

c = (a + b)/2.title: Bisection method
c = (a + b)/2.about: If f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, a continuous f must cross zero between them (intermediate value theorem). Test the midpoint c and keep the half where the sign still changes. Each step halves the bracket: slow, but it can't fail.
assumptions: f continuous on [a, b], f(a) f(b) < 0
Common slip: keeping the wrong half; keep the one whose ends still differ in sign
Misses double roots like x^{2} = 0, where f doesn't change sign

example.problem: One step on f(x) = x^{2} − 2 over [1, 2].

x_{n+1} = g(x_{n}).title: Fixed-point iteration
x_{n+1} = g(x_{n}).about: Rewrite f(x) = 0 as x = g(x) and iterate. Near the fixed point x*, e_{n+1} ≈ g′(x*) e_{n}: each step multiplies the error by g′, so it converges when |g′| < 1 and faster the smaller |g′| is. Newton's method is the choice g = x − f/f′, which makes g′(x*) = 0.

example.problem: Solve x = cos(x) from x₀ = 1.
steps: g′ = −sin x ≈ −0.67 at the root, so it zigzags in

assumptions: g continuous, start near the fixed point
Diverges where |g′| > 1; try another rearrangement (x = g(x) has many)
If g′ < 0 the iterates zigzag around the root
related: Newton, a fixed-point iteration with g′ = 0

y = y_{0} + (y_{1} − y_{0})(x − x_{0})/(.title: Linear interpolation
y = y_{0} + (y_{1} − y_{0})(x − x_{0})/(.about: Reads a value between two table entries by assuming a straight line between them. Error is about h² f″/8 for spacing h.

example.problem: A steam table gives 2.0 at 100 and 2.6 at 120. Estimate at 105.

assumptions: x_{0} ≤ x ≤ x_{1}; outside it is extrapolation and less reliable
Why: the straight line through two points; (x − x_{0})/(x_{1} − x_{0}) is the fraction of the way across
Error ≈ (x − x_{0})(x − x_{1}) f″/2, largest at mid-interval for curved data

p(x) = Σ_{i=0}^{n} y_{i} Π_{j≠i} (x − x_.title: Lagrange interpolating polynomial
p(x) = Σ_{i=0}^{n} y_{i} Π_{j≠i} (x − x_.about: The one polynomial of degree ≤ n through n + 1 points. Each basis term is 1 at its own point and 0 at the others. High degrees on evenly spaced points can wiggle badly (Runge).

example.problem: Fit (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 7) and evaluate at x = 1.5.
steps: p(x) = x^{2} + x + 1 fits all three

assumptions: All x_{i} distinct
Common slip: raising the degree to fit more evenly spaced points; past about 5 it oscillates between them (Runge). Use piecewise or spline fits instead

f′(x) ≈ (f(x) − f(x − h))/h.title: Backward difference
f′(x) ≈ (f(x) − f(x − h))/h.about: A one-sided slope using the point behind. Taylor: f(x − h) = f − hf′ + (h^{2}/2)f″ − …, so the error is about (h/2) f″: first order, halve h and the error halves. Used when only past samples exist, as in real-time data and backward Euler.

example.problem: A car's position is logged every 0.1 s as x = t^{2} m. Estimate its speed at t = 1 s from the last two samples.

assumptions: Common slip: making h tiny; below about √(machine ε)·|x| round-off in f(x) − f(x − h) dominates
Use the central difference when both neighbours exist: error O(h^{2})

∫ f dx ≈ h Σ_{i=0}^{n−1} f(x_{i} + h/2).title: Midpoint rule
∫ f dx ≈ h Σ_{i=0}^{n−1} f(x_{i} + h/2).about: Each strip uses f at its centre. Second-order accurate, with an error about half the trapezoid rule's and of opposite sign.

example.problem: Estimate ∫ x^{2} dx from 0 to 1 with the midpoint rule and n = 2.

assumptions: Common slip: evaluating at the strip ends; the midpoints are x_{i} + h/2
Needs no endpoint values, so it works for integrands that blow up at an end

E_{T} = −(b − a) h^{2} f′′(ξ)/12.title: Error of the composite trapezoid rule
E_{T} = −(b − a) h^{2} f′′(ξ)/12.about: The trapezoid rule's error shrinks with h²: halve the step and the error falls about 4 times. A convex f (f″ > 0) is overestimated.
vars: exact integral minus the trapezoid estimate

example.problem: Bound the error for ∫ e^{x} dx on [0, 1] with h = 0.1.

assumptions: f″ continuous on [a, b]
Use the largest |f″| on [a, b] for a safe bound

y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1}).title: Backward (implicit) Euler
y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1}).about: Uses the slope at the end of the step, so y_{n+1} appears on both sides and must be solved for (by algebra, or Newton's method if f is nonlinear). First-order accurate, but stable for decaying problems at any step size, which is what stiff problems need.
vars: time at the end of the step

example.problem: y′ = −10y, y₀ = 1, h = 0.5. One step.

assumptions: Common slip: plugging an old y into the right side; that is forward Euler
Stable for any h when y′ = λy with λ < 0; forward Euler needs h < 2/|λ|
related: the backward difference it rests on

y_{n+1} = y_{n} + (h/2)(f(t_{n}, y_{n}).title: Heun's method (improved Euler)
y_{n+1} = y_{n} + (h/2)(f(t_{n}, y_{n}).about: Predict the end of the step with Euler, then average the slope at the start and at that predicted end: the trapezoid rule applied to y′ = f. Averaging cancels Euler's first-order error, so it is second-order accurate: halve h and the error drops 4 times.

example.problem: y′ = y, y₀ = 1, h = 0.1. One step.

assumptions: Explicit, so it shares Euler's step-size limit on stiff problems
Common slip: using f(t_{n+1}, y_{n}) for the second slope; it needs the predicted y

A = L U.title: LU decomposition
A = L U.about: Gaussian elimination, stored: the multipliers used to clear each column become L, and the reduced matrix is U. Factor once (about n^{3}/3 operations), then each new right side costs only a forward solve Ly = b and a back solve Ux = y.

example.problem: Factor A = [4 3; 6 3], then solve A x = (10, 12).

assumptions: A square and nonsingular
A zero (or tiny) pivot breaks it; partial pivoting, PA = LU, swaps rows to fix that
Common slip: computing A^{−1} to solve Ax = b; LU is cheaper and more accurate
related: how much the answer can be trusted
iterative alternative for large sparse A

x_{i}^{(k+1)} = (b_{i} − Σ_{j≠i} a_{ij}.title: Jacobi iteration
x_{i}^{(k+1)} = (b_{i} − Σ_{j≠i} a_{ij}.about: Solve each equation for its own unknown, using the last guess for the others. Converges when A is diagonally dominant. Gauss-Seidel uses each new value at once and usually converges faster.

example.problem: 4x + y = 6, x + 3y = 7, from (0, 0). Two steps.
example.answer: (0.917, 1.833) after two steps; the solution is (1, 2)

assumptions: Converges if A is strictly diagonally dominant (each |a_{ii}| exceeds the sum of the other |a_{ij}| in its row); reorder rows to get that
Common slip: using new values within the same sweep; that is Gauss-Seidel
related: direct solve, better for small dense systems

x_{k+1} = A x_{k}/‖A x_{k}‖.title: Power method
x_{k+1} = A x_{k}/‖A x_{k}‖.about: Write the start vector as a mix of eigenvectors. Each multiply by A scales component i by λ_{i}, so the largest |λ| wins, by a factor |λ_{2}/λ_{1}| per step; dividing by the length keeps the numbers finite. The Rayleigh quotient x^{T}Ax/x^{T}x estimates that eigenvalue.
vars: vector length, to keep x_{k} from growing

example.problem: A = [2 1; 1 2], x₀ = (1, 0). Iterate three times and estimate λ.
steps: A x₀ = (2, 1), then (5, 4), then (14, 13): direction near (1, 1)
Rayleigh quotient with x = (14, 13): A x = (41, 40)

assumptions: One eigenvalue strictly largest in magnitude
x₀ needs some component along its eigenvector (a random start has one)
Slow when |λ_{2}/λ_{1}| is near 1; a negative λ₁ makes the sign flip each step
related: uses the largest and smallest singular values

|e_{n+1}| ≈ C |e_{n}|^{p}.title: Order of convergence
|e_{n+1}| ≈ C |e_{n}|^{p}.about: How fast an iteration's error shrinks. p = 1 is linear (a fixed fraction each step, as bisection), p ≈ 1.618 is the secant method, p = 2 is quadratic (Newton: the correct digits double each step).

example.problem: Newton's errors go 10^{−2}, 10^{−4}, … What comes next?

assumptions: Read p from data: p ≈ ln(e_{n+1}/e_{n})/ln(e_{n}/e_{n−1})
In practice p = 2 doubles the correct digits each step; p = 1 adds a fixed number

log_{2}(n!) ≈ n log_{2}(n).title: Lower bound for comparison sorting
log_{2}(n!) ≈ n log_{2}(n).about: Any sort that works by comparing pairs must tell apart all n! possible orderings, and each yes/no comparison at best halves the possibilities, so it needs at least log_{2}(n!) comparisons in the worst case. By Stirling, log_{2}(n!) ≈ n log_{2} n − 1.44 n, so no comparison sort beats Θ(n log n). Merge sort and heapsort meet this bound.

example.problem: At least how many comparisons does sorting 1000 items take in the worst case?
steps: The leading term alone, 1000 log_{2}(1000) ≈ 9966, overestimates by about 1.44n

assumptions: Only comparison sorts; counting, radix and bucket sorts use the keys' values and can run in Θ(n)
The row keeps the leading term n log_{2} n; the full Stirling form is n log_{2} n − n log_{2} e + O(log n)
A worst-case (and average-case) bound, not a guarantee for every input

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n).title: Merge sort recurrence
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n).about: Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half recursively and merges them in linear time. The recursion has log_{2} n levels and each level does Θ(n) merging work, so the total is Θ(n log n): case 2 of the master theorem with a = b = 2.
related: the comparison-sort lower bound it meets

example.problem: About how many basic steps does merge sort take on n = 2^{20} = 1,048,576 items?

assumptions: The same bound holds in the best, average and worst case
Needs Θ(n) extra memory for merging
Any algorithm that splits into two halves and combines in linear time has the same recurrence (e.g. FFT)

T(n) = T(n/2) + Θ(1) = Θ(log n).title: Binary search recurrence
T(n) = T(n/2) + Θ(1) = Θ(log n).about: Binary search compares the key with the middle of a sorted range and recurses on one half, so each step halves the range. It finishes in about log_{2} n steps: case 2 of the master theorem with a = 1, b = 2.

example.problem: At most how many comparisons does binary search need to find a key among 1,000,000 sorted items?

assumptions: The array must be sorted
Random access to the middle element in Θ(1) (an array, not a linked list)
Worst case ⌈log_{2}(n + 1)⌉ comparisons
related: bits, or yes/no questions, to pick one of N

E = 1/(1 − α).title: Expected probes in open addressing
E = 1/(1 − α).about: With open addressing, an unsuccessful search (or an insert) probes about 1/(1 − α) slots on average. It grows without limit as the table fills, which is why such tables resize once α passes about 0.7.
vars: load factor n/m, keys per slot

example.problem: A table with open addressing is 90% full. How many probes does an unsuccessful search expect?

assumptions: Uniform hashing: each probe sequence is equally likely
Open addressing only, so α < 1; chaining costs about 1 + α instead
A successful search costs less: (1/α) ln(1/(1 − α))

n = 2^{h+1} − 1.title: Nodes in a perfect binary tree
n = 2^{h+1} − 1.about: A perfect binary tree of height h has every level full: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^{h} nodes. Turned around, a balanced tree of n nodes has height about log_{2} n, which is why balanced-tree operations take Θ(log n).
vars: height, with the root at depth 0

example.problem: How many nodes does a perfect binary tree of height 9 hold?

assumptions: Perfect: every internal node has two children and every leaf is at depth h
Height counts edges, so a single root has h = 0
2^{h} of the nodes are leaves

E = V − 1.title: Edges in a tree
E = V − 1.about: A tree on V vertices (connected, with no cycles) always has exactly V − 1 edges. Adding any edge makes a cycle and removing any edge disconnects it. A spanning tree of a network therefore always uses V − 1 links.

example.problem: A spanning tree connects 50 cities. How many links does it use?

assumptions: Connected and acyclic; a forest of k trees has V − k edges
Undirected graph

E = V(V − 1)/2.title: Edges in a complete graph
E = V(V − 1)/2.about: In a complete graph every pair of vertices is joined, so the edges number V choose 2. It is the most edges a simple undirected graph can have, so a dense graph has Θ(V^{2}) edges and an adjacency matrix suits it.

example.problem: 20 people each shake hands once with everyone else. How many handshakes?

assumptions: Simple undirected graph (no loops, no repeated edges)
A complete directed graph has V(V − 1) edges
related: the same count as a sum
tree, the fewest for a connected graph

Σ deg(v) = 2E.title: Handshake lemma
Σ deg(v) = 2E.about: Each edge adds 1 to the degree of both its ends, so the degrees of all vertices add to twice the number of edges. It counts edges from degrees, and shows the number of odd-degree vertices is always even.
vars: degree of vertex v: edges meeting it

example.problem: A network has 10 nodes, each linked to 3 others. How many links are there?

assumptions: Undirected graph; a self-loop adds 2 to its vertex's degree
For a directed graph: Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = E

V − E + F = 2.title: Euler's formula for planar graphs
V − E + F = 2.about: A connected graph drawn in the plane with no crossing edges has V − E + F = 2, counting the outer region as a face. It is also true of the vertices, edges and faces of any convex polyhedron, and it gives E ≤ 3V − 6, which proves K_{5} is not planar.

example.problem: A planar graph has 8 vertices and 12 edges. How many faces does it have?

assumptions: Connected and drawn without crossings; with k components V − E + F = 1 + k
F includes the unbounded outer face
E ≤ 3V − 6 needs a simple graph with V ≥ 3

0 ≤ x ≤ 2^{n} − 1.title: Range of an unsigned integer
0 ≤ x ≤ 2^{n} − 1.about: n bits hold 2^{n} patterns, read as the whole numbers 0 up to 2^{n} − 1. Use it to pick a type that won't overflow: past the top an unsigned counter wraps around to 0.

example.problem: What is the largest value of a 16-bit unsigned integer?

assumptions: Plain binary, no sign bit
Common sizes: 8 bits to 255, 16 to 65,535, 32 to 4,294,967,295

−2^{n−1} ≤ x ≤ 2^{n−1} − 1.title: Range of a two's complement integer
−2^{n−1} ≤ x ≤ 2^{n−1} − 1.about: Signed n-bit integers in two's complement give half the 2^{n} codes to negative numbers, so there is one more negative value than positive. The top bit is the sign; negate a value by flipping every bit and adding 1. Going past the top wraps around to the most negative value.
vars: number of bits, including the sign bit

example.problem: What range does a signed 8-bit integer hold?

assumptions: Two's complement, the format of every modern CPU
−(−2^{n−1}) overflows back to itself

S = (1 − p) + p N.title: Gustafson's law: scaled speedup
S = (1 − p) + p N.about: The speedup when the problem grows with the machine: with N processors, if a fraction p of the parallel run's time is spent in parallel work, the same run would take (1 − p) + pN times as long on one processor. It is a more hopeful view than Amdahl's fixed-size law for big simulations.
vars: parallel fraction of the parallel run's time

example.problem: A simulation spends 95% of its run time in parallel work on 64 processors. What is its scaled speedup?

assumptions: p is the parallel share of the time measured on the N-processor run (Amdahl's p is a share of the serial run)
The problem size grows with N (weak scaling)
Ignores communication overhead

L = λ W.title: Little's law
L = λ W.about: In a system in steady state, the average number of items inside equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside. It holds for any queue, server, store or pipeline, whatever the arrival pattern, so knowing two of the three gives the third.

example.problem: A server gets 200 requests per second and each spends 50 ms in it. How many requests are in progress on average?

assumptions: Steady state: the long-run arrival rate equals the departure rate
Averages over a long time; it says nothing about the spread
λ and W in matching time units
related: the same idea for bits in flight

d = d_{proc} + d_{queue} + d_{trans} + d.title: Total delay at one network hop
d = d_{proc} + d_{queue} + d_{trans} + d.about: A packet's delay at each hop is the sum of four parts: processing at the router, waiting in the queue, pushing its bits onto the link (L/R) and travelling the link (distance/speed). Add the hops for end-to-end delay.

example.problem: A 1500-byte packet crosses a 100 Mbit/s link 2000 km long (signal speed 2 × 10^{8} m/s), with no queue and negligible processing. Find the delay.

assumptions: d_{trans} depends on packet size and link rate, d_{prop} on distance only
d_{queue} varies with traffic and is often the largest and least predictable part
Store-and-forward: each hop receives the whole packet before sending it on

w = (X^{T} X + λI)^{−1} X^{T} y.title: Ridge regression, closed form
w = (X^{T} X + λI)^{−1} X^{T} y.about: Least squares with an L2 penalty λ‖w‖^{2}, solved in one step. Adding λI keeps X^{T}X invertible even with correlated or too many features, and shrinks the weights toward zero, trading a little bias for less variance (less overfitting).
vars: data matrix, one row per example (n × d)

example.problem: One feature, no intercept: X = [1; 2], y = [1; 2] and λ = 1. Find the ridge weight.

assumptions: λ ≥ 0; λ = 0 is ordinary least squares, larger λ shrinks more
Standardize the features first, since the penalty treats every weight alike
The intercept is usually not penalized: centre the data or leave its entry of I as 0
Choose λ by cross-validation

ŷ = σ(w · x + b).title: Logistic regression
ŷ = σ(w · x + b).about: A linear score w · x + b squashed by the sigmoid into the probability that x belongs to the positive class. It is the standard first model for yes/no classification; it is trained by minimising binary cross-entropy, and its decision boundary w · x + b = 0 is a line or plane.

example.problem: A model gives an email the score w · x + b = 2. What probability of spam does it predict?

assumptions: Two classes; softmax extends it to more
The log-odds ln(ŷ/(1 − ŷ)) are linear in the features
Predict class 1 when ŷ > 0.5 (z > 0), or another threshold chosen for the costs

d(x, y) = √(Σ (x_{i} − y_{i})^{2}).title: Euclidean distance
d(x, y) = √(Σ (x_{i} − y_{i})^{2}).about: The straight-line distance between two feature vectors: Pythagoras in as many dimensions as there are features. k-nearest neighbours and k-means use it to decide which points are close.

example.problem: Find the distance between the feature vectors (1, 2, 3) and (4, 6, 3).

assumptions: Scale the features first (standardize or min-max), or the one with the largest range dominates
In very many dimensions distances bunch together, so it discriminates less; cosine similarity is often used for embeddings

σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)).title: Derivative of the sigmoid
σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)).about: The slope of the sigmoid can be written with its own value, so backpropagation gets it almost for free from the forward pass. It peaks at 0.25 at z = 0 and goes to 0 for large |z|, the vanishing-gradient problem of deep sigmoid networks.

example.problem: Find the sigmoid's slope at z = 0 and at z = 4.

assumptions: At most 0.25, so each sigmoid layer shrinks the gradient at least fourfold

tanh(z) = (e^{z} − e^{−z})/(e^{z} + e^{−.title: Hyperbolic tangent activation
tanh(z) = (e^{z} − e^{−z})/(e^{z} + e^{−.about: An S-curve from −1 to 1, centred on 0. Because its outputs average near zero it often trains better than the sigmoid, and it is the usual activation inside recurrent networks (LSTM, GRU).

example.problem: What does a tanh unit output for an input of 1?

assumptions: Saturates for large |z|, so it also suffers vanishing gradients
tanh(z) = 2σ(2z) − 1: a rescaled sigmoid

A = softmax(Q K^{T}/√(d_{k})) V.title: Scaled dot-product attention
A = softmax(Q K^{T}/√(d_{k})) V.about: The core operation of transformers. Each query scores every key by a dot product, scaled by √d_{k} so the scores don't grow with dimension and push softmax into saturation; the softmax of each row gives weights that average the value vectors. The result is each token's context-weighted mix of the others.
vars: query matrix, one row per query
key matrix, one row per key
value matrix, one row per key
dimension of the keys and queries

example.problem: One query q = (1, 0) attends to keys (1, 0) and (0, 1), with d_{k} = 2. Find the attention weights.

assumptions: Softmax is taken along each row (over the keys for one query)
Q is n × d_{k}, K is m × d_{k}, V is m × d_{v}; the output is n × d_{v}
A mask sets disallowed scores to −∞ (e.g. future tokens) before the softmax

RMSE = √(MSE).title: Root mean squared error
RMSE = √(MSE).about: The square root of the mean squared error, which puts the typical prediction error back in the target's own units. It punishes large errors more than MAE does; RMSE ≥ MAE always.

example.problem: A model's errors on three examples are 1, −2 and 3. Find the RMSE.

assumptions: Sensitive to outliers, like MSE
Compare RMSE only between models on the same target and data

MAE = (1/n) Σ |y_{i} − ŷ_{i}|.title: Mean absolute error
MAE = (1/n) Σ |y_{i} − ŷ_{i}|.about: The average size of the prediction errors, in the target's units. It is less sensitive to outliers than MSE, and a model minimising it predicts the median rather than the mean.

example.problem: A model's errors on three examples are 1, −2 and 3. Find the MAE.

assumptions: Not differentiable at zero error; optimizers use a subgradient or the Huber loss
All errors count in proportion to their size

R^{2} = 1 − SS_{res}/SS_{tot}.title: Coefficient of determination (R squared)
R^{2} = 1 − SS_{res}/SS_{tot}.about: The share of the target's variance that a model explains. 1 is a perfect fit, 0 is no better than always predicting the mean ȳ, and a negative value is worse than that.
vars: total sum of squares about the mean

example.problem: A model leaves a residual sum of squares of 20 on data whose total sum of squares is 100. Find R^{2}.
example.answer: R^{2} = 0.8: the model explains 80% of the variance

assumptions: Adding features never lowers R^{2} on the training data; use adjusted R^{2} or a validation set
For a one-feature least-squares line R^{2} = r^{2}

L = −(y ln(ŷ) + (1 − y) ln(1 − ŷ)).title: Binary cross-entropy (log loss)
L = −(y ln(ŷ) + (1 − y) ln(1 − ŷ)).about: The loss for yes/no classifiers that output a probability ŷ. Only one term survives: −ln ŷ when the truth is 1, −ln(1 − ŷ) when it is 0. Confident wrong answers cost a lot. Average it over the examples.

example.problem: The true label is y = 1. Find the loss when the model says ŷ = 0.9, and when it says ŷ = 0.1.

assumptions: y is 0 or 1; ŷ is strictly between 0 and 1 (clip it, or compute from the logit)
With a sigmoid output its gradient with respect to the logit is simply ŷ − y
Natural log gives nats

L = max(0, 1 − y ŷ).title: Hinge loss
L = max(0, 1 − y ŷ).about: The support vector machine's loss. It is zero once an example is on the right side of the boundary with a margin of at least 1, and rises linearly otherwise, so training only cares about the examples near or across the boundary.

example.problem: An example has label y = 1. Find the hinge loss when its score ŷ is 2, 0.5 and −1.
steps: ŷ = 0.5: max(0, 1 − 0.5) = 0.5, right side but inside the margin

assumptions: Labels are y = ±1, not 0/1
ŷ is the raw score w · x + b, not a probability
Usually paired with an L2 penalty on w, which sets the margin width

L + λ ‖w‖_{1}.title: L1 regularization (lasso)
L + λ ‖w‖_{1}.about: Adds λ times the sum of the absolute weights to the loss. Unlike L2 it drives many weights to exactly 0, so it selects features as well as shrinking them.

example.problem: A model has loss 0.40 and weights (0.5, −0.2, 0). With λ = 0.1, what is the regularized loss?

assumptions: The bias is usually not penalized
Standardize the features first
Choose λ by validation; with correlated features it tends to keep one and drop the rest

G = 1 − Σ p_{i}^{2}.title: Gini impurity
G = 1 − Σ p_{i}^{2}.about: How mixed the classes are at a decision-tree node: the chance that two examples drawn at random from it belong to different classes. It is 0 for a pure node and at most 1 − 1/k for k classes (0.5 for two). CART trees pick the split that lowers the size-weighted impurity most.
vars: fraction of class i at the node

example.problem: A node holds 70% class A and 30% class B. Find its Gini impurity.

assumptions: p_{i} is the fraction of the node's examples in class i; they sum to 1
Behaves much like entropy, and is cheaper (no logs)

IG = H(parent) − Σ (n_{k}/n) H(child_{k}.title: Information gain
IG = H(parent) − Σ (n_{k}/n) H(child_{k}.about: How much a split lowers the entropy of a decision-tree node: the parent's entropy minus the children's, each weighted by its share of the examples. ID3 and C4.5 split on the feature with the largest gain.

example.problem: A node of 8 examples, 4 of each class, splits into one child with 3 A and 1 B and another with 1 A and 3 B. Find the information gain.

assumptions: H = −Σ p log_{2} p, in bits
Favours features with many values; C4.5 divides by the split's own entropy (gain ratio) to correct this

v ← β v + ∇L, w ← w − η v.title: Gradient descent with momentum
v ← β v + ∇L, w ← w − η v.about: Keeps a running, decaying sum v of past gradients and steps along it. Along a direction where the gradient keeps the same sign the steps grow up to 1/(1 − β) times larger; across a zigzagging valley the alternating signs cancel. β ≈ 0.9 is typical.

example.problem: The gradient stays at 1 every step and β = 0.9. What does the velocity v settle at?
steps: At steady state v = βv + 1, so v = 1/(1 − β)
example.answer: v = 10: steps up to 10 times those of plain gradient descent

assumptions: β between 0 and 1; β = 0 is plain gradient descent
Some libraries write v ← βv + (1 − β)∇L, which changes the effective learning rate by 1/(1 − β)

w ← w − η m̂/(√(v̂) + ϵ).title: Adam optimizer
w ← w − η m̂/(√(v̂) + ϵ).about: Adam keeps running averages of the gradient (m) and of its square (v), corrects their bias toward zero in the first steps, and divides one by the root of the other. Each weight so gets its own step size of about η, whatever the scale of its gradient. It is the default optimizer for deep networks.
vars: bias-corrected average of the squared gradient
small constant against division by zero

example.problem: For one weight m̂ = 0.2, v̂ = 0.04 and η = 0.001. How far does the weight move?
example.answer: 0.001: Adam's steps are about η in size

assumptions: m ← β_{1}m + (1 − β_{1})∇L, v ← β_{2}v + (1 − β_{2})(∇L)^{2}, all element by element
Bias correction: m̂ = m/(1 − β_{1}^{t}), v̂ = v/(1 − β_{2}^{t}) at step t
related: v ← β v + ∇L,  w ← w − η v

x′ = (x − x_{min})/(x_{max} − x_{min}).title: Min-max normalization
x′ = (x − x_{min})/(x_{max} − x_{min}).about: Rescales a feature linearly so the training set's smallest value maps to 0 and its largest to 1. It puts features on a common scale for distance-based models and neural networks; standardization (z-score) is the alternative when there are outliers.

example.problem: Ages in the training set run from 18 to 68. Scale an age of 43.

assumptions: Use the training set's x_{min} and x_{max} for the test data too; test values may fall outside [0, 1]
One outlier squeezes everything else into a narrow band

TNR = TN/(TN + FP).title: Specificity (true negative rate)
TNR = TN/(TN + FP).about: Of all the real negatives, the fraction the model correctly calls negative. It pairs with recall (sensitivity): a medical test needs both, high sensitivity to catch the disease and high specificity to avoid false alarms.

example.problem: Of 100 healthy patients, a test clears 90 and wrongly flags 10. Find its specificity.

assumptions: Undefined if there are no real negatives
Specificity = 1 − FPR

FPR = FP/(FP + TN).title: False positive rate
FPR = FP/(FP + TN).about: Of all the real negatives, the fraction wrongly flagged positive: 1 − specificity. The ROC curve plots recall against FPR as the decision threshold moves; the area under it (AUC) summarises the classifier.

example.problem: Of 100 legitimate emails, a filter wrongly flags 10 as spam. Find its false positive rate.

assumptions: Undefined if there are no real negatives
Not the same as the share of positive calls that are wrong (that is 1 − precision)
related: true positive rate, the ROC curve's y-axis

EAR = (1 + r/n)^{n} − 1.title: Effective annual rate (APY)
EAR = (1 + r/n)^{n} − 1.about: What a nominal annual rate compounded n times a year really earns in a year. Compare loans and accounts by their effective rate, not the quoted APR.

example.problem: A card charges 12% APR compounded monthly. What is the effective annual rate?

assumptions: r is the nominal annual rate (APR) as a decimal
For continuous compounding EAR = e^{r} − 1
Fees are not included

FV = PV (1 + r)^{n}.title: Future value of a single sum
FV = PV (1 + r)^{n}.about: How much a sum invested today grows to after n periods at a compound rate r per period. It is the inverse of discounting.

example.problem: $1000 is invested at 5% a year for 10 years. What is it worth then?

assumptions: r per period and n in the same periods (monthly rate with months)
Interest is reinvested at the same rate; no deposits or withdrawals

PV = FV e^{−r t}.title: Continuous discounting
PV = FV e^{−r t}.about: The present value of an amount due at time t when interest compounds continuously at rate r: the inverse of A = P e^{rt}. It is the discounting used in option pricing and continuous-time models.

example.problem: $10,000 is due in 5 years. What is it worth today at 4% continuously compounded?

assumptions: r is a continuously compounded annual rate, constant
t in years

B = P (1 + r)^{k} − M ((1 + r)^{k} − 1)/.title: Loan balance after k payments
B = P (1 + r)^{k} − M ((1 + r)^{k} − 1)/.about: How much is still owed on an amortizing loan after k payments: the loan grown with interest, less the payments, each grown with interest since it was made. Use it to find the payoff amount or the equity built after some years.
related: the balance equals the PV of the remaining payments

example.problem: A $200,000, 30-year loan at 0.5% a month has a payment of $1199.10. What is owed after 60 payments?

assumptions: Fixed rate r per payment period, fixed payment M at the end of each period
M is the payment from M = P r/(1 − (1 + r)^{−n})
Early payments are mostly interest, so the balance falls slowly at first

PV = C/r.title: Perpetuity
PV = C/r.about: The present value of a payment C every period forever, starting one period from now. It values a preferred share, a consol bond or an endowment that pays out only its interest.

example.problem: An endowment pays $5000 a year forever. What is it worth at 4%?
steps: First payment one year from now, forever

assumptions: Constant payment and rate, r > 0
The first payment is one period from now; add C for a payment today
r per payment period

PV = C/(r − g).title: Growing perpetuity (Gordon growth model)
PV = C/(r − g).about: The present value of payments that start at C one period from now and grow at rate g forever. As a stock valuation (the Gordon growth model) the price is P_{0} = D_{1}/(r − g), with D_{1} next year's dividend.
assumptions: r > g, or the value is infinite
C is the next payment, not the one just paid (D_{1} = D_{0}(1 + g))
Constant growth forever: very sensitive to r − g

example.problem: A stock will pay a $2 dividend next year, growing 3% a year. Investors require 8%. What is it worth?

E[R] = r_{f} + β (E[R_{m}] − r_{f}).title: Capital asset pricing model (CAPM)
E[R] = r_{f} + β (E[R_{m}] − r_{f}).about: The return investors should expect from an asset: the risk-free rate plus β times the market risk premium. β measures how strongly the asset moves with the market (β = 1 moves with it, β = 2 twice as much). It sets the cost of equity used in WACC and in valuations.

example.problem: The risk-free rate is 4%, the market is expected to return 10%, and a stock has β = 1.2. What return should it offer?

assumptions: Only market (systematic) risk is rewarded; risk that diversification removes is not
β is estimated from past returns: β = Cov(R, R_{m})/Var(R_{m})
All rates over the same period, as decimals

S = (R_{p} − r_{f})/σ_{p}.title: Sharpe ratio
S = (R_{p} − r_{f})/σ_{p}.about: Excess return per unit of risk: how much a portfolio earns above the risk-free rate for each unit of volatility. Higher is better when comparing portfolios or funds.
vars: standard deviation of the portfolio return

example.problem: A fund returned 12% with 16% volatility while the risk-free rate was 4%. Find its Sharpe ratio.

assumptions: R_{p}, r_{f} and σ_{p} over the same period (annualize σ by √12 from monthly)
Treats all volatility as risk and assumes roughly normal returns

WACC = (E/V) r_{E} + (D/V) r_{D} (1 − T).title: Weighted average cost of capital
WACC = (E/V) r_{E} + (D/V) r_{D} (1 − T).about: A firm's blended cost of money: the costs of equity and debt weighted by their market values. Interest is tax-deductible, hence the (1 − T) on debt. It is the discount rate for projects as risky as the firm as a whole.

example.problem: A firm has $60M of equity costing 10% and $40M of debt at 5%, with a 25% tax rate. Find its WACC.

assumptions: V = E + D at market values, not book values
r_{E} often from CAPM; r_{D} is the pre-tax yield on the firm's debt
The project has the same risk and financing mix as the firm

P = Σ_{t=1}^{n} C/(1 + y)^{t} + F/(1 + y.title: Bond price
P = Σ_{t=1}^{n} C/(1 + y)^{t} + F/(1 + y.about: The price of a bond is the present value of its coupons and its face value, discounted at its yield. When yields rise, prices fall; a bond whose coupon rate equals its yield sells at par (its face value).

example.problem: A 3-year bond has a $1000 face value and a 5% annual coupon. What is it worth at a 6% yield?
example.answer: P ≈ $973.27 (below par, since the yield exceeds the coupon)

assumptions: C and y per coupon period (halve both for semiannual coupons, and double n)
Priced on a coupon date; between dates add accrued interest
The yield to maturity is the y that makes this equal the market price

PM = (R − C)/R.title: Profit margin
PM = (R − C)/R.about: The share of each dollar of revenue the business keeps as profit. Which costs go into C sets the kind: cost of goods only gives gross margin, all costs and taxes give net margin.

example.problem: A firm has $500k of revenue and $420k of costs. Find its profit margin.

assumptions: R and C over the same period
Margin is a share of the price; markup (R − C)/C is a share of the cost, and is larger

D = (C − S)/n.title: Straight-line depreciation
D = (C − S)/n.about: Spreads an asset's cost, less what it can be sold for at the end of its life, evenly over its years of service. The simplest depreciation method, used in accounting and engineering economics.

example.problem: A $50,000 machine will be sold for $5000 after 9 years. Find the annual depreciation.

assumptions: Equal depreciation every year
S is the estimated salvage (residual) value at the end of the useful life
Book value after k years: C − kD

c = 2r sin(θ/2).title: Chord length from the central angle
c = 2r sin(θ/2).about: The straight-line distance between two points on a circle that subtend a central angle θ. Halving the isosceles triangle from the centre gives a right triangle with hypotenuse r and opposite side c/2.
assumptions: θ is the central angle between the two radii (degrees or radians, as long as sin is taken in the same unit)
For the curved distance along the circle use the arc length s = rθ
related: arc length on the same angle

example.problem: A circle of radius 10 cm has a chord subtending 60° at the centre. How long is the chord?

A = π(R^{2} − r^{2}).title: Area of an annulus (ring)
A = π(R^{2} − r^{2}).about: The area between two concentric circles: the big circle less the hole. Use it for washers, pipe and tube cross-sections and ring-shaped plates.
assumptions: Concentric circles, R the outer radius and r the inner, R ≥ r
With diameters: A = π(D^{2} − d^{2})/4

example.problem: A washer has an outer diameter of 40 mm and a 20 mm hole. Find its face area.

A = (1/2) d_{1} d_{2}.title: Area of a rhombus or kite from its diagonals
A = (1/2) d_{1} d_{2}.about: A rhombus or kite has perpendicular diagonals, which cut it into four right triangles whose areas add to half the product of the diagonals.
assumptions: The diagonals must be perpendicular (rhombus, kite, square); not for a general parallelogram
A rhombus can also use base × height

example.problem: A kite has diagonals of 12 cm and 9 cm. Find its area.

V = (1/3) πh(R^{2} + R r + r^{2}).title: Volume of a frustum (truncated cone)
V = (1/3) πh(R^{2} + R r + r^{2}).about: A cone with its tip cut off parallel to the base, like a bucket, lampshade or tapered column. It is the big cone less the small one, written in the two radii and the height between them.
assumptions: The cut is parallel to the base; h is the perpendicular height of the frustum, not the slant height
With r = 0 it is a cone; with r = R a cylinder
For a pyramid frustum: V = (h/3)(A_{1} + √(A_{1}A_{2}) + A_{2})

example.problem: A bucket is 30 cm tall, 15 cm in radius at the top and 10 cm at the bottom. How much does it hold?

360°/n.title: Exterior angle of a regular polygon
360°/n.about: Walking once around any convex polygon turns you through 360° in all, so each of the n equal exterior angles of a regular polygon is 360°/n. The interior angle is 180° minus it.
assumptions: Regular (equal sides and angles) for each angle to be 360°/n; the 360° total holds for any convex polygon
Interior angle = 180° − 360°/n = (n − 2)180°/n

example.problem: Find each exterior and interior angle of a regular hexagon.

A_{2}/A_{1} = k^{2}, V_{2}/V_{1} = k^{3.title: Scaling of similar figures
A_{2}/A_{1} = k^{2}, V_{2}/V_{1} = k^{3.about: If every length of a figure is multiplied by k, its areas (including surface area) scale by k^{2} and its volumes (and mass, at the same density) by k^{3}. Use it for similar triangles, scale models and map scales.
assumptions: The figures are similar: same shape, every length scaled by the same factor k
k = (a length in figure 2)/(the matching length in figure 1)

example.problem: A 1:20 scale model of a tank holds 3 L. How much does the full-size tank hold?

θ_{i} = θ_{c}/2.title: Inscribed angle theorem
θ_{i} = θ_{c}/2.about: An angle with its vertex on a circle is half the central angle that stands on the same arc. So every inscribed angle on the same arc is equal, and an angle inscribed in a semicircle is 90° (Thales).
assumptions: The vertex is on the circle and both angles stand on the same arc
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°
vars: inscribed angle, vertex on the circle
central angle on the same arc
related: arc length from the central angle

example.problem: An arc subtends 110° at the centre of a circle. What angle does it subtend at a point on the rest of the circle?

IQR = Q_{3} − Q_{1}.title: Interquartile range and the 1.5 IQR outlier rule
IQR = Q_{3} − Q_{1}.about: The spread of the middle half of the data, from the first quartile to the third. Unlike the standard deviation it ignores extreme values, so it pairs with the median; a value more than 1.5 IQR below Q_{1} or above Q_{3} is flagged as an outlier (the box-plot fences).
assumptions: Q_{1} and Q_{3} are the 25th and 75th percentiles; textbooks and software differ slightly in how they interpolate them
Fences: Q_{1} − 1.5 IQR and Q_{3} + 1.5 IQR
related: standard deviation, the other measure of spread

example.problem: Test scores have Q_{1} = 62 and Q_{3} = 80. Is a score of 110 an outlier?
example.answer: IQR = 18; the fence is 107, so 110 is an outlier

z = (p̂ − p_{0})/√(p_{0}(1 − p_{0})/n).title: One-proportion z test
z = (p̂ − p_{0})/√(p_{0}(1 − p_{0})/n).about: Tests whether a population proportion differs from a claimed value p_{0}: how many standard errors the sample proportion lies from p_{0}. Compare z with the critical value (1.96 for a two-sided test at 5%) or find its p-value.
assumptions: Random sample, independent observations
Large enough: n p_{0} ≥ 10 and n(1 − p_{0}) ≥ 10
The standard error uses p_{0}, not p̂ (the confidence interval uses p̂)
vars: proportion claimed by the null hypothesis

example.problem: A coin lands heads 60 times in 100 tosses. Test at 5% whether it is fair (p_{0} = 0.5).

t = (x̄_{1} − x̄_{2})/√(s_{1}^{2}/n_{1}.title: Two-sample t test (Welch)
t = (x̄_{1} − x̄_{2})/√(s_{1}^{2}/n_{1}.about: Tests whether two independent groups have different means: the difference of the sample means over its standard error. Use it to compare a treatment with a control, or two machines or methods.
assumptions: Two independent random samples; for paired data (before/after on the same subjects) use a one-sample t test on the differences
Each population roughly normal, or each n large (about 30+)
Welch’s form does not assume equal variances; its degrees of freedom come from the Welch–Satterthwaite formula, or conservatively min(n_{1}, n_{2}) − 1

example.problem: Machine A: n = 25 parts, mean 50.2 mm, s = 0.5 mm. Machine B: n = 25, mean 49.9 mm, s = 0.6 mm. Is the difference in means significant at 5%?

Σ_{i=1}^{n} 1/i ≈ ln(n) + 0.5772.title: Harmonic series (harmonic numbers)
Σ_{i=1}^{n} 1/i ≈ ln(n) + 0.5772.about: The sum 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/n grows like ln n, plus Euler’s constant γ ≈ 0.5772. It appears in the average cost of quicksort (about 2n ln n comparisons), the coupon-collector problem (n H_{n} draws to see all n items) and the expected number of times a running maximum changes.
assumptions: The approximation is good to about 1/(2n)
It diverges: there is no finite sum to infinity, only slow log growth

example.problem: A cereal brand hides one of 50 toys in each box at random. On average, how many boxes collect all 50?

E = 1 + α.title: Expected search cost with chaining
E = 1 + α.about: With separate chaining, each slot holds a linked list of the keys that hash there, averaging α keys. A search hashes once and walks the list, so its expected cost is Θ(1 + α): constant time as long as the table grows with n.
assumptions: Simple uniform hashing
An unsuccessful search walks a whole chain, about 1 + α; a successful one about 1 + α/2
Chaining allows α > 1, unlike open addressing

example.problem: A chained hash table holds 3000 keys in 1000 slots. About how many nodes does an unsuccessful search examine?

MIPS = f/(CPI × 10^{6}).title: MIPS rating
MIPS = f/(CPI × 10^{6}).about: Millions of instructions completed per second: the clock rate divided by the average cycles per instruction. Handy for quick comparisons, but misleading across different instruction sets, where one instruction does different amounts of work.
assumptions: CPI averaged over the actual instruction mix
Only fair between machines running the same instruction set and program; compare run times otherwise

example.problem: A 2.5 GHz processor averages 1.25 cycles per instruction. What is its MIPS rating?

S = C/(B k).title: Number of sets in a cache
S = C/(B k).about: A cache of C bytes stores blocks (lines) of B bytes, so it holds C/B blocks; grouped k to a set, that makes C/(B k) sets. Direct-mapped is k = 1, fully associative is one set holding every block.
assumptions: C, B in the same unit (bytes); all three are powers of 2
The set count fixes the index bits, log_{2} S

example.problem: A 32 KiB, 4-way set-associative cache has 64-byte blocks. How many sets does it have?

t = a − log_{2}(S) − log_{2}(B).title: Splitting an address into tag, index and offset
t = a − log_{2}(S) − log_{2}(B).about: A cache splits each a-bit address into three fields: the low log_{2} B bits pick the byte within a block (offset), the next log_{2} S bits pick the set (index), and the rest are the tag stored to check for a hit.
assumptions: Byte-addressed memory; S and B powers of 2
Fully associative: S = 1, so no index bits
Total storage adds the tag, valid (and dirty) bits to each block

example.problem: A 32-bit address goes to a cache with 128 sets of 64-byte blocks. How many bits are tag, index and offset?

U = (L/R)/(RTT + L/R).title: Stop-and-wait link utilization
U = (L/R)/(RTT + L/R).about: In stop-and-wait, the sender transmits one packet (taking L/R) and then sits idle until its acknowledgement returns an RTT later. The fraction of time the link is busy is tiny on long, fast links, which is why pipelined protocols (Go-Back-N, selective repeat, TCP windows) send W packets at once, raising U up to W times.
assumptions: No losses; acknowledgement transmission time ignored
RTT is the round-trip propagation time
With a window of W packets: U = W(L/R)/(RTT + L/R), at most 1

example.problem: A 1 Gb/s link has a 30 ms RTT. Find the stop-and-wait utilization for 1000-byte packets.

ŷ = argmax_{y} P(y) Π_{i} P(x_{i} | y).title: Naive Bayes classifier
ŷ = argmax_{y} P(y) Π_{i} P(x_{i} | y).about: Picks the class with the largest posterior from Bayes’ theorem, assuming the features are independent given the class, so the likelihood is a product of one-feature probabilities. Fast and strong for text (spam filters) even when the assumption is false.
assumptions: Features conditionally independent given the class (the naive part)
P(x) is the same for every class, so it is dropped
Use logs to avoid underflow, and add-one (Laplace) smoothing so an unseen word does not zero the product
vars: prior: share of training examples in class y
probability of feature i given class y

example.problem: 40% of email is spam. "Free" appears in 30% of spam and 2% of ham; "meeting" in 1% of spam and 5% of ham. Is an email containing both words spam?

margin = 2/‖w‖.title: Margin of a support vector machine
margin = 2/‖w‖.about: A linear SVM separates classes with the hyperplane w · x + b = 0 and scales w so the closest points (the support vectors) satisfy w · x + b = ±1. The gap between those two planes is 2/‖w‖, so maximizing the margin means minimizing ‖w‖^{2}.
assumptions: Hard margin: the data are linearly separable; a soft margin adds the hinge loss with a penalty C
Labels y = ±1, constraint y(w · x + b) ≥ 1
vars: width of the gap between the classes
weight vector, normal to the hyperplane

example.problem: A trained SVM has w = (3, 4). How wide is its margin?

J = Σ_{i} ‖x_{i} − μ_{c_{i}}‖^{2}.title: k-means objective (within-cluster sum of squares)
J = Σ_{i} ‖x_{i} − μ_{c_{i}}‖^{2}.about: k-means puts n points into k clusters to make J, the total squared distance from each point to its cluster’s centroid, small. It alternates two steps that each lower J: assign every point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points. Plot J against k and look for the elbow to choose k.
assumptions: k is chosen beforehand; the result depends on the starting centroids (use k-means++ or several restarts)
Euclidean distance: scale the features first
Finds round clusters of similar size; it reaches a local, not global, minimum
vars: centroid of the cluster point i is in

example.problem: Points 1, 2 and 6 on a line form one cluster. Find its centroid and its share of J.

λ_{k}/(Σ_{i} λ_{i}).title: PCA explained variance ratio
λ_{k}/(Σ_{i} λ_{i}).about: Principal component analysis rotates centred data onto the eigenvectors of its covariance matrix. Each eigenvalue λ_{k} is the variance along component k, so λ_{k}/Σ λ_{i} is the share of the total variance it keeps. Keep enough components to reach, say, 90–95% in total.
assumptions: Centre the data (subtract each feature’s mean); standardize too if features have different units
Eigenvalues sorted largest first; the sum of all λ_{i} equals the total variance (the trace of the covariance matrix)
vars: eigenvalue k of the covariance matrix: variance along component k

example.problem: A covariance matrix has eigenvalues 4.2, 1.5, 0.2 and 0.1. How much variance do the first two components explain?

n_{out} = (n + 2p − k)/s + 1.title: Convolution (and pooling) output size
n_{out} = (n + 2p − k)/s + 1.about: The width (or height) of the feature map a convolution or pooling layer produces from an n-wide input with a k-wide kernel, p padding on each side and stride s. Round the division down when it isn’t whole.
assumptions: Apply to width and height separately; the depth out is the number of filters
"Same" padding with s = 1 is p = (k − 1)/2, which keeps n_{out} = n
Parameters of a conv layer: (k × k × channels in + 1) × filters

example.problem: A 224 × 224 image goes through a 7 × 7 convolution with stride 2 and padding 3. What size is the output?

E[(y − ŷ)^{2}] = Bias^{2} + Var + σ^{2}.title: Bias-variance decomposition
E[(y − ŷ)^{2}] = Bias^{2} + Var + σ^{2}.about: The expected squared error of a model on new data splits into bias squared (error from too simple a model: underfitting), variance (error from sensitivity to the training set: overfitting) and the irreducible noise σ^{2}. More complex models trade bias for variance; regularization and more data cut variance.
assumptions: Squared-error loss; the expectation is over training sets and noise at a fixed x
σ^{2} is the noise in y itself, which no model can remove
vars: average prediction minus the true value
variance of the prediction across training sets

example.problem: A model has bias 0.3 and prediction variance 0.05, on data with noise variance 0.1. What is its expected squared error?

∇_{w} L = (ŷ − y) x.title: Gradient of the loss for one example
∇_{w} L = (ŷ − y) x.about: For logistic regression with the log loss, and for a linear model with the loss (1/2)(ŷ − y)^{2}, the gradient with respect to the weights is the error times the input. It is the core of backpropagation’s last layer and of every gradient descent step on these models.
assumptions: Logistic: ŷ = σ(w · x + b) with binary cross-entropy; linear: ŷ = w · x + b with (1/2) squared error
The bias gradient is ŷ − y
Over a batch, average the per-example gradients
vars: gradient of the loss with respect to the weights

example.problem: A logistic model predicts ŷ = 0.8 for an example with x = (1, 2) and y = 0. With η = 0.1, how does w change?

PV_{due} = (1 + r) PMT (1 − (1 + r)^{−n}.title: Present value of an annuity due
PV_{due} = (1 + r) PMT (1 − (1 + r)^{−n}.about: An annuity due pays at the start of each period (rent, leases, insurance premiums), so every payment arrives one period earlier than in an ordinary annuity and is worth (1 + r) times as much.
assumptions: r is the rate per payment period and n the number of payments
The future value of an annuity due is likewise (1 + r) times the ordinary FV

example.problem: A 5-year lease costs $10,000 a year paid at the start of each year. What is it worth today at 6%?

Σ C_{t}/(1 + IRR)^{t} = 0.title: Internal rate of return (IRR)
Σ C_{t}/(1 + IRR)^{t} = 0.about: The discount rate that makes a project’s NPV zero: its own rate of return. Accept a project when its IRR beats the required return (the cost of capital). Except in simple cases it is found by trial or a solver.
assumptions: C_{0} is the (negative) initial outlay at t = 0
Cash flows that change sign more than once can give several IRRs; then rely on NPV
To rank projects of different size, use NPV, not IRR
vars: net cash flow at period t
internal rate of return per period

example.problem: You invest $1000 now and receive $1210 in 2 years. What is the IRR?

PP = I/C.title: Payback period
PP = I/C.about: How long a project takes to earn back its initial cost: the cost over the yearly cash flow when the flows are even. With uneven flows, add them up year by year until they cover the cost.
assumptions: Even yearly cash flows for the formula
Ignores the time value of money (the discounted payback period fixes this) and everything after payback, so it can favour poor projects; use NPV to decide

example.problem: A $45,000 machine saves $12,000 a year. What is its payback period?

E[R_{p}] = Σ w_{i} E[R_{i}].title: Expected return of a portfolio
E[R_{p}] = Σ w_{i} E[R_{i}].about: The weighted average of the assets’ expected returns, weighted by the share of money in each. Unlike risk, return does not benefit from diversification: it is just the average.
assumptions: Weights w_{i} are fractions of the portfolio value and add to 1 (a negative weight is a short position)
All returns over the same period
vars: share of the portfolio in asset i

example.problem: A portfolio is 60% stocks expected to return 9% and 40% bonds expected to return 4%. What is its expected return?

σ_{p}^{2} = w_{1}^{2}σ_{1}^{2} + w_{2}^{.title: Variance of a two-asset portfolio
σ_{p}^{2} = w_{1}^{2}σ_{1}^{2} + w_{2}^{.about: The risk of a mix of two assets. The cross term carries the correlation ρ: unless ρ = 1, the portfolio is less volatile than the weighted average of the two volatilities. That gap is the benefit of diversification.
assumptions: σ_{1}, σ_{2} are the standard deviations of the returns; ρσ_{1}σ_{2} is their covariance
The portfolio standard deviation is the square root

example.problem: Stocks (σ = 20%) and bonds (σ = 8%) with ρ = 0.2 are held 60/40. Find the portfolio standard deviation.

CY = C/P.title: Current yield of a bond
CY = C/P.about: The annual coupon divided by the bond’s market price: the income return alone. It ignores the gain or loss as the price moves to face value at maturity, which the yield to maturity includes.
assumptions: C is the annual coupon in dollars (coupon rate × face value)
P is the market price, not the face value
related: bond price and yield to maturity

example.problem: A $1000 bond with a 5% coupon trades at $973.27. What is its current yield?

B_{k} = C (1 − d)^{k}.title: Declining-balance depreciation
B_{k} = C (1 − d)^{k}.about: Each year the asset loses a fixed fraction d of its remaining book value, so depreciation is largest early on. Double-declining balance uses d = 2/n for an n-year life, twice the straight-line rate.
assumptions: Year k’s depreciation is d B_{k−1}
The book value never reaches zero on its own; firms switch to straight line or stop at the salvage value
Tax rules (such as MACRS) use their own tables

example.problem: A $50,000 machine with a 5-year life is depreciated by double-declining balance. What is its book value after 2 years?

n ≥ log_{2}((b − a)/ε).title: Bisection: iterations for a tolerance
n ≥ log_{2}((b − a)/ε).about: Each bisection step halves the bracket, so after n steps the midpoint is within (b − a)/2^{n} of the root. Solving for n gives how many steps reach a tolerance ε before you start.
assumptions: f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a), f(b) have opposite signs
Round n up to the next whole number
It counts steps, each one f evaluation

example.problem: How many bisections find a root in [1, 2] to within 10^{−6}?

x_{k+1} = x_{k} − J^{−1}(x_{k}) F(x_{k}).title: Newton's method for a system of equations
x_{k+1} = x_{k} − J^{−1}(x_{k}) F(x_{k}).about: Newton's method in several unknowns: linearize F at the current guess with its Jacobian matrix J and step to where that linear model is zero. In practice solve J Δx = −F(x_k) and set x_{k+1} = x_k + Δx; don't invert J.
assumptions: F is differentiable and J is invertible near the root
Converges quadratically from a close enough guess; can diverge from a poor one
vars: vector of equations set to zero
Jacobian matrix of F at x_k

example.problem: Take one Newton step for x^{2} + y^{2} = 4, x = y from (1, 1).

f[x_{0}, x_{1}] = (f(x_{1}) − f(x_{0}))/.title: Divided difference
f[x_{0}, x_{1}] = (f(x_{1}) − f(x_{0}))/.about: The first divided difference is the slope between two data points; higher ones are divided differences of divided differences, f[x₀, x₁, x₂] = (f[x₁, x₂] − f[x₀, x₁])/(x₂ − x₀). They are the coefficients of Newton's interpolating polynomial, built in a triangular table.
assumptions: The x values are distinct; they need not be evenly spaced
f[x₀, …, x_{n}] ≈ f^{(n)}/n! for close points

example.problem: Find f[1, 3] for f(x) = x^{2}.

p(x) = f[x_{0}] + f[x_{0}, x_{1}](x − x_.title: Newton's divided-difference interpolating polynomial
p(x) = f[x_{0}] + f[x_{0}, x_{1}](x − x_.about: The polynomial through n + 1 data points, written so each new point adds one term. Its coefficients are the top diagonal of the divided-difference table. It is the same polynomial as Lagrange's, but easier to extend and to evaluate.
assumptions: Distinct x values
Degree n through n + 1 points; high degree on evenly spaced points can oscillate (Runge)

∫ f dx ≈ (3h/8)(f_{0} + 3f_{1} + 3f_{2}.title: Simpson's 3/8 rule
∫ f dx ≈ (3h/8)(f_{0} + 3f_{1} + 3f_{2}.about: Fits a cubic through four equally spaced points and integrates it. Use it when the number of intervals is a multiple of 3, or with Simpson's 1/3 rule to cover an odd number of intervals.
assumptions: Equally spaced points, h = (b − a)/3 for one panel
Error O(h^{4}), like the 1/3 rule; exact for cubics
Composite: weights 1, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3, 2, …, 3, 1
vars: f at x_{i} = a + i h

∫_{−1}^{1} f dx ≈ f(−1/√3) + f(1/√3).title: Two-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature
∫_{−1}^{1} f dx ≈ f(−1/√3) + f(1/√3).about: Picks the two sample points and weights that make the rule exact for every cubic, so two function values do the work of Simpson's three. Map [a, b] to [−1, 1] with x = ((b − a)t + a + b)/2, and multiply by (b − a)/2.
assumptions: f smooth; error depends on f^{(4)}
The points are the roots of the Legendre polynomial P₂; n points are exact to degree 2n − 1
Needs f at chosen points, not at tabulated data

E_{S} = −(b − a) h^{4} f^{(4)}(ξ)/180.title: Error of the composite Simpson's rule
E_{S} = −(b − a) h^{4} f^{(4)}(ξ)/180.about: Bounds how far Simpson's 1/3 rule is from the integral: it shrinks with h^{4}, so halving h cuts it 16 times. Bound |f^{(4)}| by M on [a, b] to get |E| ≤ (b − a) h^{4} M/180, and solve for the h or n you need.
assumptions: f has a continuous fourth derivative on [a, b]
n even, h = (b − a)/n
Exact for cubics, since then f^{(4)} = 0

x_{i}^{(k+1)} = (b_{i} − Σ_{j<i} a_{ij}.title: Gauss-Seidel iteration
x_{i}^{(k+1)} = (b_{i} − Σ_{j<i} a_{ij}.about: Solves A x = b by sweeping through the equations, solving the ith for x_i, and using each new value as soon as it is found. It usually converges about twice as fast as Jacobi, which waits for the whole sweep.
assumptions: Converges if A is strictly diagonally dominant or symmetric positive definite; reorder rows to make the diagonal large
Stop when successive iterates agree to the tolerance
